events.excerpt: Discussion topic for EIP-8477: Recent Block Bound Delegation Authorizations . Motivated by the recent EIP-7702 sweeps that happened on Binance 16 this proposal in essence prevents long term storage of EIP-7702 signatures for later playback. This proposal limits the delayed use of unused EIP-7702 authorizations. Each authorization signs a recent execution block number and its block header hash, in addition to the existing chain ID, delegation address, and nonce. For inclusion in execution block N , the signed block must be one of its preceding 256 ancestors and its hash must match that ancestor. An anchor exactly 256 blocks behind remains eligible; one 257 blocks behind is ineligible. The current block and future blocks are excluded. Freshness is checked during native authorization processing, before signature recovery or authority-specific state access. An expired or mismatched anchor skips that authorization using EIP-7702’s existing skip-on-failure behavior. It does not consume the authority’s nonce through that entry or clear an existing delegation. Structurally malformed authorizations invalidate the transaction. events.excerpt: The regression test the Fellowship added for the dotUSD incident fits on one screen. Alice holds 1,000 dotUSD and no DOT. She sends one WithdrawAsset for her dotUSD plus 1 DOT. dotUSD sorts first and gets withdrawn, the DOT withdrawal fails, the instruction errors. Before the fix, her balance came back and the supply didn’t. Parity’s incident review went up yesterday ( review ) and explains it at a high level. I wanted to see both halves in code, the supply that drifted and the pool that priced it, so I read the fix in polkadot-sdk and that test ( tests.rs at 7b27d43 ). All of it is fixed and public, and I’m only looking at the code here, not at the disclosure timeline. The credit that dropped too late Since polkadot-sdk PR #10384 (merged 16 February 2026) the XCM executor keeps real imbalances in holding instead of plain numbers. That PR was actually written to keep total issuance correct during XCM programs. WithdrawAsset takes each asset from the origin as a Credit and collects them in a local called withdrawn . withdrawn was declared before TransactionalProcessor::process(|| ...) and only moved into holding in an .and_then after it. events.excerpt: Between 24 and 26 October 2026, a bug in the XCM executor on Polkadot Asset Hub was used to reduce the recorded issuance of dotUSD without changing underlying account balances. The recorded issuance is expected to equal the sum of all account balances. By reducing the recorded issuance without changing any account’s balance, the attacker broke this assumption within the protocol. This discrepancy affected pricing in the Hub’s DOT/dotUSD pool on the decentralised exchange and enabled trades at an artificial exchange rate. The estimated loss was approximately $1.381 million in DOT value. At the time of the attack, the Polkadot Treasury was the only liquidity provider in the pool. No users lost any funds. The available on-chain evidence has not established that the attacker who exploited the XCM vulnerability also profited from the subsequent arbitrage. Furthermore, the bug did not remove dotUSD from account balances, but the understated recorded issuance restricted redemption capacity pending a correction. What happened XCM programs are meant to be transactional. That is, when a program fails, none of the state changes from that program are applied. There was a bug present that did not follow this behavior in certain circumstances. The issue was first reported to Parity through its

events.excerpt: TL;DR: XCMv3 will be removed in polkadot-sdk stable2612 (release 2026-12-17, ingestion by fellowship runtimes only after that). Once system chains upgrade, they will no longer send or accept v3 messages. If your chain or your app still uses v3, you need to move to v4 or v5 before then. Check your chain on the dashboard: XCM Versions . XCMv5 was merged in November 2024: XCM v5 by franciscoaguirre · Pull Request #4826 · paritytech/polkadot-sdk · GitHub . A PR removing v3 ( Remove XCMv3 by franciscoaguirre · Pull Request #13629 · paritytech/polkadot-sdk · GitHub ) will ship in stable2612 , scheduled for 2026-12-17 . After that, system parachains and any other runtime can adopt it. Allowing for runtime releases and governance, expect the first chains to drop v3 in early 2027. Once a chain drops v3, it can’t decode v3 messages sent to it and can’t downgrade outgoing messages to v3. XCM between that chain and any other chain still on v3 will fail. To help, I built a dashboard ( XCM Versions ) showing each chains’ XCM version. Click a chain to see suggested action items. The main ones are: Code: move XCM programs and types to v4+. This is mostly renames (e.g. dropping the Multi prefix). Raw v3 types in storage don’t need migrating because the encoding is the same, but stored Versioned*

events.excerpt: ⚠️ Security: CVE-2026-98432 (Linux kernel) CVE-2026-98432 is a use-after-free in the Linux kernel's IPv4 TCP stack. It is not specific to MPTCP, but the demonstrated remote exploit requires an MPTCP listener, which Go 1.24+ enables by default. This release disables MPTCP listeners in lnd by default , which closes the demonstrated exploit path through lnd. It is a mitigation, not a fix: the kernel patch is the only fix. Linux operators should: Upgrade to this release. Disable MPTCP on the host ( sudo sysctl -w net.mptcp.enabled=0 ), since other services on the machine are not covered by this release. Install a patched kernel as soon as your distribution ships one. If you cannot upgrade yet, start your existing binary with the environment variable GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0 , which turns off Go's default MPTCP listeners. Do not set GODEBUG=multipathtcp=1 to re-enable MPTCP until your kernel is patched. The Go team's discussion of the issue is at golang/go#82717 . See the release notes for the full instructions, including Docker and firewall guidance. Windows and macOS are not affected. Database Migrations There are no migrations in this release. events.excerpt: A Kusama Wish for Change needs a 666.67 KSM decision deposit before it can go to a vote. Governance takes that deposit from one account. A proposal can have support and still time out because nobody can carry the whole amount. We have built a contract that lets people and groups share it. The first pool is live for our Wish for Change #676 . We are asking for code review and people to try the Paseo rehearsal. This is experimental and has not had an independent review. We deployed before that review to leave time before #676 times out. A killed referendum loses the deposit, and a contract bug could also put contributions at risk. Kusama pool : real KSM. Paseo rehearsal : free test PAS. Source, tests and logs . Verified Kusama contract . How it works Each pool is fixed to one referendum and its exact deposit. It has no owner, admin key or upgrade path. People contribute from their own accounts. The payment that fills the pool tries to place the deposit in the same transaction. If placement fails, the contribution stays in the pool and anyone can retry. Contributors can withdraw while the pool remains open, before placement. After the referendum ends, anyone can reclaim the deposit and send payouts to the contributing accounts. These are separate contract calls. No watcher is runnin
events.headline: Collaborative decision deposits: live on Kusama, open for review

events.excerpt: Disclaimer: This is an independent proposal from an ordinary Cosmos community member. I am not affiliated with Cosmos Labs, the Interchain Foundation, or the Cosmos Hub development team. This is not an official initiative or a finalized technical specification. My intention is to share an idea and gather community feedback. TL;DR I would like to propose exploring ATOM Shield , a limited emergency freezing mechanism for native ATOM on the Cosmos Hub. The goal is to prevent stolen ATOM from being moved further during major security incidents, without halting the entire network, while leaving final decisions to decentralized governance. The proposed mechanism would work as follows: 1 Security Council member: Initiates an immediate freeze lasting up to 1 hour. Additional Council approval: Extends the freeze for up to 24 hours from the initial action. At least 2/3 of all active Council members within 24 hours: Confirms the freeze until governance reaches a decision. Cosmos Hub governance: Decides whether to unfreeze, maintain the freeze, or authorize recovery of the assets. Failure to meet approval thresholds: Results in automatic unfreezing. events.excerpt: At 8:08am HKT, 30th October 2026, the Security Council executed an emergency action to freeze 8,425 ETH and 74,559,805.2 ARB held on Arbitrum One by an address identified with today’s Binance exploit. The funds are now held at 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000DA0 . The funds can only be moved by an ArbitrumDAO Governance vote, which will be coordinated with relevant parties. Key point: Funds associated with the Binance exploit are frozen on Arbitrum One. No other user’s funds or applications were affected. Security Council Actions The technical approach taken by the Security Council was to implement an atomic action to upgrade the inbox contract on Ethereum, freeze the funds, and return the contract back to its original implementation. The Inbox Contract was upgraded to add a new function, sendUnsignedTransactionOverride , which imitates the structure of a standard cross-chain transaction with the ability to impersonate the transaction sender. Two cross-chain transactions were created to impersonate the address associated with the Binance exploit, and these transactions transferred the stolen funds to 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000DA0 . events.excerpt: Reth v2.9.0 replaces revm with evm2 as reth's EVM ( #25002 ). This is a breaking change for SDK users who build on reth's EVM, executor or inspector types. Node operators don't need to change any config. The release also fixes engine, RPC, storage and pipeline-unwind bugs, adds snap sync progress metrics and JIT support in reth-bb, and makes builds noticeably lighter by cutting monomorphization and unused dependencies. evm2 makes block execution about 10% faster than revm. On 500 mainnet blocks, execution throughput rose +10.0% and median block execution time fell 10.5%. On 300M-gas big blocks, throughput rose 9.3%, and 6.6% with BALs. Action Required SDK users: revm types are replaced by evm2 ( evm2 , evm2-inspectors , evm2-jit ). Custom EVMs, precompiles, inspectors and executors need porting to evm2's APIs. events.excerpt: Introduction This forum thread is for communicating activity for the Osero Configurator Bounded External Access Module (cBEAM), maintained as required by A.2.2.10.1.1.1.2.4.1.4.2 — Public Communication . A cBEAM is a whitelisted Operator of a Diamond Parallelized Allocation Unit (Diamond PAU). It can, for example, use the Configurator to adjust that unit’s rate limits within the ceilings set by BeamState, without requiring a Spell or waiting for the GSM Pause Delay, as specified in A.1.10.3.2.10.5 — cBEAM Exception and A.2.2.10.1.1.1.2.4.1.4.1 — Operator Execution . The Operator for the Osero Diamond PAU is specified in A.2.2.10.1.1.1.2.4.1.4.3.2 — Operator For The Osero Diamond PAU . Sky Governance maintains full control over cBEAM actions through Executive Votes or Core Council actions . The Core Council Multisig can immediately unpair a cBEAM from a RateLimits contract or Controller, or remove its registration, as specified in A.2.2.10.1.1.1.2.4.1.3.4 — Immediate Function Calls . Configurator operations can also be halted through A.2.2.10.1.1.1.2.4.1.3.6 — PASMom . events.excerpt: Introduction For the upcoming launch of Spark’s DPAU on Base, we’re also launching PAS/Configurator there to be able to adjust DPAU rate limits and remove facets in an emergency, same as on Arbitrum . The Beacon was deployed by Spark themselves; we’re just ensuring its state is correct. Goal of this update Allow trusted operator groups (coreCouncil and cBEAM) to make changes to Spark’s Diamond PAU module on Base without requiring a spell. Initially, the module will be launched with Timelock paused (same as on Ethereum Mainnet and Arbitrum One ), still requiring core L2 spells to perform the most security-critical operations. Required context Spark is planning to launch their second instance of DPAU in “parallel configuration”, meaning that the new Diamond PAU controller, rate limits, and facets will be sharing the existing ALMProxy with the legacy Controller already holding funds. As an additional precaution, we recommend attaching the PAS/Configurator module to the DPAU to be able to slowly ramp up its rate limits and also remove the onboarded facet in case of emergency. events.excerpt: Two threads here this month made me look at the same problem from both ends. In one , a holder has ATOM on UX Chain, which halted in July, and RoboMcGobo explained why the Hub can’t just release it: the escrow only opens when the other chain burns the voucher, and that chain makes no blocks. In the other, Akash’s proposal 346 (voting until 2 November) starts a migration that ends with akashnet-2 halting 90 days after a later cutover. So I went through ibc-go (v10.7.0, the version Gaia v29.0.1 runs; akashnet-2 runs v10.5.0, and the transfer code I cite is the same there) to list what has to happen before the last block, because after it nobody can fix anything from the other side. This is not about whether any chain should leave. It’s only about the tokens. Why tokens get stuck When a token leaves its home chain, it goes into that chain’s escrow for the channel and the other side mints a voucher. The escrow releases it only when a packet shows the voucher was burned, and that packet has to come from a live chain. Transfer channels can’t be closed. The transfer module rejects ChanCloseInit , so there is no close-and-settle step. Every packet, ack and timeout is checked through the counterparty’s light client, and the client has to be Active.
